creator: Alexander Terp
description:
A literal `{` in a string produces an error naming the symptom and nothing about the cause. #153 hit it twice, in both string flavors:

```rad
if ch in `\.+*?()[]{}|^$`:
// error[RAD10001]: Expected identifier
// error[RAD20028]: Undefined identifier ''

if t.starts_with("{"):
// error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '"{"'
```

Both times the author reached the fix by inference. A hint naming the interpolation rule and its two exits, `\{` and `r`-strings, routes them straight there.

Backticks make it worse: they're the recommended delimiter for shell and regex-flavored strings, which primes an expectation of raw-string behavior they don't deliver.

Worth handling the adjacent trap in the same pass, because a hint saying "use an r-string" walks the reader into it. `r` suppresses interpolation entirely, so ``$r`echo "{payload}"` `` ships `{payload}` to the shell as literal text. The prefix that fixes the parse-time problem quietly breaks the interpolation-time one - #153 calls that adjacency the thing that cost the time.

Same family while the error surface is open: a `\` line continuation gives `error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '\'`. If continuations are deliberately out, one clause saying so settles it instead of leaving the author to wonder whether they mistyped.

---

### Scope after the sibling card
`a_25S3ICERd` ("Let an unambiguous literal brace parse") now owns the *semantics* change. Once it lands, both of the transcripts quoted above stop being errors: `` `\.+*?()[]{}|^$` `` parses because the `{}` pair is empty, and `t.starts_with("{")` parses because the `{` is immediately followed by the terminator.

This card is purely about **message text for the cases that remain errors**:

1. `"{name"` - a forgotten closing brace, in every string flavor.
2. `\` used as a line continuation.

### Orientation
- This is checker/parser-diagnostic work in `rts`, not the interpreter. Parse errors become messages in `rts/check/error_messages.go`, reached from `RadCheckerImpl.addInvalidNodes` (`rts/check/check.go:192`), which walks the tree-sitter ERROR nodes.
- Diagnostics carry an optional `Suggestion` (`rts/check/structs.go:46`), rendered as a `= help:` line. That is the slot a hint goes in.
- There is direct precedent for exactly this kind of targeted rescue: `checkUnterminatedString` (`rts/check/error_messages.go:783`) and `checkMultilineStringIndent` (`rts/check/error_messages.go:757`). Both take an ERROR node, recognise a specific misshape, and return `(msg, code, *suggestion)` in place of the generic message.

### Current output, verified against a freshly built `bin/radd`
Forgotten closing brace, identical in both flavors:
```
print("{name")   ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '{name'
print(`{name`)   ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '{name'
```
The span points at `{name`, so the diagnostic already knows exactly which text it is unhappy about - it just doesn't say why. This is the message to rewrite.

Line continuation:
```
x = 1 + \       ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '\'   (emitted twice, same position)
    2
```
The duplicate is worth collapsing in the same pass. `computeMisorderedSwitchSuppressionRanges` (`rts/check/check.go:200`) is the existing precedent for de-duplicating an ERROR cascade.

### What the hint should name
Verified: `\{` works today - `print("\{name}")` prints `{name}` - and it is documented at `SYNTAX.md:913`. Also verified: `{{` is **not** an escape; `print("{{")` gives `error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '"{{"'`. So the hint names `\{`, and does not invent a second escape.

The discovery gap is the whole point of this card: the escape exists and is documented, and #153's author reached for r-strings twice without ever finding it.

### Watch out for
- **Sequencing with `a_25S3ICERd`.** Write the detector to key on `{` followed by identifier-like content that runs to the string terminator without a `}`, not on "any ERROR node near a brace". A broad matcher written before the sibling lands will start firing on the cases the sibling is about to make legal.
- `rts` must not import `core` - it sits upstream of both `core` and `radls`. Everything here stays inside `rts/check`, which is also what makes the hint appear in editors.
- `addInvalidNodes` runs off the tree-sitter CST, not the AST: `c.ast` is nil whenever syntax is invalid (`rts/check/check.go:58-65` swallows the converter panic), so an AST-based check will never fire for these cases.
title: Teach the interpolation parse errors to name the rule
